overview: Great Moravia was a ninth-century political formation ruled by the Mojmirid dynasty. Mikulcice preserves evidence of its centres, including bridges, churches, workshops and food remains. Slavic literary work accompanied religious and diplomatic change. Its political collapse in the early tenth century did not erase the population or every settlement; the map's 900-1000 interval is not its historical lifetime.

periods.title: Centres of government, craft and religion
periods.summary: Ninth-century Mikulcice combined fortifications, bridges, residential quarters and churches. Its material remains reveal a complex centre supported by farming, skilled work and exchange.

periods.title: Political collapse and local continuity
periods.summary: Great Moravia collapsed in the early tenth century amid internal conflict and Magyar pressure. Reduced settlement continued at Mikulcice. The whole century must not be read as continued existence of the earlier state.

sections.title: Building and moving through a river landscape

items.text: Mikulcice occupied raised ground within the Morava floodplain. Its ninth-century defences combined timber and earth with a stone-facing wall. Waterways shaped both access and protection, making engineering part of everyday movement through the settlement.

Archaeologists found wooden bridge remains in former river channels around Mikulcice. These crossings connected the fortified core with surrounding occupied areas, giving physical evidence of routes that no longer follow today's river course.

The Czech archaeological atlas records a Great Moravian dugout canoe lifted at Mikulcice in 1967. The surviving vessel complements the bridge evidence for movement on and across water; 1967 dates its recovery, not its construction.

The acropolis contained a basilica and a building interpreted as a palace, while residential quarters extended into the outer bailey and beyond. Churchyards and burials help reconstruct institutions, but the entire population did not live inside the elite core.

sections.title: Food, farming and differences within society

items.text: Mikulcice's plant remains include millet, wheat, rye, barley and oats. Millet dominates seed counts, but the archaeobotanical study shows that rankings change when weight and food value are considered. Many small seeds do not automatically mean most calories.

Grape pips survived at Mikulcice as charred, mineralised and waterlogged remains. Their shapes raise questions about wild grapes and older cultivated varieties. Finding pips establishes grape use more securely than a particular vineyard, wine recipe or grape variety.

A study of adults buried by Mikulcice's Church VI compared tooth and bone chemistry from the same people. The researchers interpreted the differences as more millet and less animal protein in childhood than adulthood, recovering changes within individual lives.

The same study linked inferred social position with dietary differences, including greater animal-protein consumption among the elite. These findings concern the sampled cemetery population, rather than proving a uniform diet across all of Great Moravia.

Great Moravian pottery includes both specialist workshop products and simpler domestic manufacture. The archaeological institute stresses that techniques changed at different speeds and served different customers, rather than replacing all older practices at once.

A ninth-century silver chain earring from Mikulcice illustrates fine metalworking. Other elite jewellery used filigree and granulation alongside simpler ornaments. Finished objects show technical skill, but do not by themselves establish whether knowledge travelled with visiting artisans or returning apprentices.

The institute also illustrates a ninth-century antler playing piece from Mikulcice decorated with a bowman. This small object adds leisure and imagery to a record often dominated by churches, weapons and prestigious graves.

Constantine, later called Cyril, developed Glagolitic letters for Slavic religious writing. With Methodius, he helped build a literary and teaching tradition tied to Moravia's church diplomacy. Their mission entered a region where Christian institutions already existed.

ending.text: The Mojmirid political structure collapsed in the early tenth century under Magyar pressure and internal strain. This ended a state, not its entire society. Reduced occupation at Mikulcice and the later reuse of Moravian identity make total depopulation an unsuitable description; the exact sequence remains debated.

sources.title: Czech archaeological atlas, Mikulcice
sources.note: Site description and image captions: acropolis, outer bailey, basilica, residential areas and a dugout canoe lifted in 1967. The excavation date is not the boat's manufacture date.

sources.title: Lumir Polacek and colleagues, Great Moravian Elites From Mikulcice
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology, Czech Academy of Sciences, Brno, 2020. Pages 21 and 50: political collapse, Magyar pressure, internal conflict and population continuity; pp. 64-65 and 163: Constantine, Methodius and Slavic literary work. Approximate collapse is not a verified single fall day.

sources.title: Michaela Latkova, The Archaeobotany of Mikulcice: Food Supply to the Early Medieval Stronghold
sources.note: 2017, pp. 52-53: grain counts, weight and dietary importance; p. 58 and plates 5-6: grape pips and problems distinguishing wild grapes from cultivars. Preservation and seed size affect interpretation.

sources.title: Michaela Jilkova and colleagues, Early medieval diet in childhood and adulthood at Mikulcice
sources.note: Archives of Oral Biology, 2019, abstract Design, Results and Conclusion. Church VI cemetery: 91 adult skeletons, paired tooth and bone analysis. Childhood diet is reconstructed from adult remains, not a separate sample of children.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology, Czech Academy of Sciences, Transfer of technologies and ideas
sources.note: Paragraphs on specialist and domestic pottery, jewellery, granulation and filigree; ninth-century Mikulcice chain earring and antler playing-piece captions. Transmission mechanisms remain an open research question.
